reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / WHO Classification of Endocrine Tumours
clinicalPearls: The most common thyroid malignancy, typically presenting as a painless thyroid nodule or an incidentally detected lesion on imaging in a euthyroid patient

Diagnosis rests on the characteristic nuclear features rather than architecture: ground-glass 'Orphan-Annie eye' nuclei, nuclear grooves, and intranuclear pseudo-inclusions, often with laminated psammoma bodies
Spreads preferentially via lymphatics to cervical nodes, so palpable or ultrasound-detected nodal disease at presentation is common and does not preclude cure
Ultrasound features suggesting malignancy include marked hypoechogenicity, microcalcifications, irregular margins, and a taller-than-wide shape, prompting fine-needle aspiration
Driven by MAPK-pathway activation, most often BRAF V600E point mutation or RET/PTC rearrangements, which increasingly inform prognosis and targeted therapy
Overall prognosis is excellent, particularly in younger patients, with management centred on surgery (lobectomy or total thyroidectomy), selective radioactive iodine, and TSH suppression
Follow-up uses serum thyroglobulin as a tumour marker together with neck ultrasound to detect recurrence after thyroidectomy
reference.pathophysiology: Papillary thyroid carcinoma arises from follicular epithelial cells and is defined by distinctive nuclear changes produced by constitutive activation of the MAPK signalling cascade, most commonly through the BRAF V600E mutation or RET/PTC gene rearrangements. These oncogenic drivers promote proliferation while cells retain many features of thyroid differentiation, including iodine handling and thyroglobulin production, which underpins the utility of radioactive iodine and thyroglobulin monitoring. The tumour characteristically invades intrathyroidal lymphatics, giving multifocal disease and early spread to regional cervical lymph nodes, whereas distant haematogenous metastasis is comparatively uncommon.
additionalDifferentials: Benign colloid or hyperplastic thyroid nodule
Follicular thyroid carcinoma or follicular adenoma
Hashimoto thyroiditis with a dominant nodule
additionalInvestigations: Neck ultrasound characterising the nodule and mapping cervical lymph node compartments
Ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration with cytology reported by the Bethesda system
Serum TSH and thyroid function to confirm euthyroid status before intervention
Serum thyroglobulin and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies as a baseline and post-operative marker
Molecular testing of indeterminate aspirates for BRAF and other MAPK-pathway alterations
Cross-sectional imaging of the neck when bulky nodal or extrathyroidal extension is suspected
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging mass, hoarseness, or vocal-cord palsy suggesting extrathyroidal invasion of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
Fixed mass with stridor, dysphagia, or airway compromise
Evidence of distant metastasis such as pulmonary or skeletal deposits
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally excellent, especially in younger patients with intrathyroidal disease, where long-term survival is the norm; older age, extrathyroidal extension, large tumour size, and distant metastases are the main adverse factors.
pitfalls: Assuming cervical lymph node involvement implies a poor outcome, when nodal disease is common and compatible with cure
Relying on nodule size alone rather than suspicious sonographic features to select nodules for aspiration
Overlooking multifocality and the contralateral lobe when planning the extent of surgery
Interpreting serum thyroglobulin without accounting for interfering anti-thyroglobulin antibodies
references: WHO Classification of Endocrine and Neuroendocrine Tumours
management: Surgical resection is the mainstay, with thyroid lobectomy for low-risk intrathyroidal tumours or total thyroidectomy for larger or higher-risk disease, plus compartment-oriented neck dissection for proven nodal metastases
Selective radioactive iodine ablation after total thyroidectomy in intermediate- and high-risk disease to treat residual thyroid tissue and micrometastases
Levothyroxine for thyroid hormone replacement with TSH suppression titrated to recurrence risk
Long-term surveillance with serum thyroglobulin and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies together with neck ultrasound to detect recurrence
Targeted systemic therapy for radioiodine-refractory or progressive disease using kinase inhibitors, including BRAF- or RET-directed agents guided by molecular testing
Management within an endocrine and thyroid multidisciplinary team
